## The neuron and the action potential

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="1"}
![](images/rat_cortical_neuron_scales.png){width="80%" fig-align="left"}
<br> A cortical neuron with relevant scales
:::
:::
::: {.column .fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="2" width="50%"}
#### Action potentials represented as [spike times]{.fragment .highlight-red data-fragment-index="3"}
<div class="r-stack">
![](images/action_pot_without%20spikes.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%"}

![](images/action_pot_with%20spikes.png){.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="3" width="100%"}
Action potentials obtained from a neuron*
</div>
:::

:::

<div class="" style="position:absolute; bottom:-20px; right:20px; font-size:0.6em; color:gray;">
Nawrot MP et al. (2007)
</div>



::: notes
The brain is one of the most complex biological systems, comprising billions of interconnected neurons and supporting cells. These neural networks underlie everything we do—from perception and memory to movement and decision-making.

Neurons are highly specialized cells with complex morphology and unique physiological properties. Here I show the morphology of a neuron showing specific structures such dendrites, soma and axons and their spatial scales.

They communicate through brief electrical signals known as action potentials, which last only a few milliseconds. These action potentials arise from the flow of ions across the neuronal membrane and are typically represented as discrete events in time, called spikes (as the shape of them are nearly invariant)
:::

One of the fundamental goals of neuroscience is to understand how neurons transform external stimuli into meaningful patterns of spiking activity. To achieve this, we develop models that can predict neuronal responses to previously unseen stimuli.

For example, In sensory neuroscience, the ultimate objective is to predict how neurons respond to natural stimuli from an organism's environment.

## Spatio-temporal Receptive Field

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
<video src="images/hw_cat_rf.mp4" controls width="100%"></video>
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Region in the sensory space that modulates the response of a neuron
![](images/rf.png){width="100%"}
:::

:::
:::

<div class="" style="position:absolute; bottom:20px; right:20px; font-size:0.6em; color:gray;">
Hubel and Wiesel (1958)
</div>

::: notes
Early landmark experiments by Hubel and Wiesel demonstrated that neurons are not equally responsive to all stimuli. In this experiment, moving bars of light were presented across the visual field of a cat while recording from neurons in the visual cortex. As you'll hear from the clicking sounds, some stimulus locations evoked much stronger responses than others.

This observation led to the concept of the spatiotemporal receptive field—the region of sensory space and time over which a stimulus influences a neuron's response.

:::


## Linear description to predict neural responses

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Linear Stage
![](images/rf.png){width="100%"}

<div class="stack-eq">
$$
{\mathcal{L}} (t) = 
\iiint dxdyd\tau\,
\mathcal{K}(x,y,\tau)\,
\mathcal{S}(x,y,t-\tau)
$$
</div>

:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
Non-linear stage
![](images/nonlinear.png){width="100%"}

<div class="stack-eq">
$$
\lambda(t) = f(\mathcal{L}(t))
$$
</div>

:::


::: {.column width="25%"}
Probabilistic spiking
![](images/prob.png){width="100%"}
<div class="stack-eq">
$$
\mathrm{Spike} = \begin{cases}
         1 & \text{if } \lambda(t) > x_r \\
        0 & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
$$
</div>

:::
:::

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal{K} \sim \text{Receptive Field}
}
$$

<div class="" style="position:absolute; bottom:20px; right:20px; font-size:0.6em; color:gray;">
Schwartz et al. 2006
</div>

::: notes
We can formalize this relationship using a computational framework called the Linear–Nonlinear–Poisson, or LNP, model. In this model, the stimulus is first filtered by a linear kernel that captures the neuron's spatiotemporal preferences. The filtered output is then passed through a nonlinear function to produce an instantaneous firing rate, from which spikes are generated probabilistically using a Poisson process.

Therefore, estimating the receptive field essentially means estimating this linear filter, which allows us to predict neuronal responses to new stimuli.
:::


## RF estimation <span class="underline-fragment fragment" data-fragment-index="1">using reverse correlation studies</span>

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}

<div class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1">

- Spatio-temporal uncorrelated (white) stimulus ensemble

</div>

<div class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="3">

- Collect stimulus frames preceding each spike

</div>

<div class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="4">

- Average the stimulus ensemble (Spike-Triggered Average)

</div>

<div class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="5">

- Estimate higher-order structure using Spike-Triggered Covariance

</div>

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

<div class="r-stack">

![](images/rev_corr_1.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1" width="100%"}

![](images/rev_corr_2.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%"}

![](images/rev_corr_3.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="3" width="100%"}

![](images/rev_corr_4.png){.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="4" width="100%"}

![](images/rev_corr_5.png){.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="5" width="100%"}

</div>

::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="4"}

<div class="stack-eq">

$$
\mathrm{STA}(\tau)=
\frac{1}{N_s}
\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}
\mathbf{s}(t_i-\tau)
$$

</div>

:::

:::

:::

<div style="position:absolute; bottom:20px; right:20px; font-size:0.6em; color:gray;">
Schwartz et al. (2006)
</div>

::: notes
Given this forward model, the inverse problem naturally follows. Instead of predicting spikes from a known receptive field, we now ask: Can we recover the receptive field from the observed spikes?

Since we assume that neuronal firing depends on the presented stimulus, the stimulus and the spikes are correlated. This allows us to perform reverse correlation analysis.

In practice, we present a large ensemble of spatially and temporally uncorrelated stimuli, record the neuron's spike times, and collect the stimulus frames that preceded each spike. Averaging these frames yields the Spike-Triggered Average (STA), which provides an estimate of the neuron's linear receptive field.

More advanced methods, such as Spike-Triggered Covariance (STC), can identify additional stimulus features that contribute to the neuronal response. However, in this thesis, I focus primarily on the Spike-Triggered Average as the key method for recovering spatiotemporal receptive fields.

:::

## The Scientific Question
Previous experimental methods lack:

- Fine spatio-temporal resolution
- Long term stimulation and recording capabilities
- Experimental flexibility and affordability

<div class="card" style="font-size:1.1em; padding:1.2em;">
Can a
[flexible experimental platform]{.fragment .highlight-red}
using a
[biological surrogate of the brain]{.fragment .highlight-blue}
reveal how neuronal structure relates to function?

</div>

::: notes
 Although years of work has gone into understanding such receptive fields using both theoretical and experimental models, the biggest caveat that all previous methods lack 
Fine spatial-temporal resolution
Long term non-invasive recording capabilities
Experimental flexibility and affordability 
So the main aim of my thesis was asking the following question :
Can we use a controllable and flexible experimental platform which uses a biological surrogate of the brain to probe neuronal stimulus selectivity, or receptive fields, and use these measurements to gain insight into neuronal structure and function?

:::

## Inferring RF from forward models 

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](images/receptive_field_filters_hor.png){.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="1" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
![](images/lnp_stas.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%"}
Recovered STAs
:::
:::

::: notes
Before moving to the experimental platform and the biological results, I would first like to demonstrate that the analysis pipeline performs as expected.
To validate the receptive field estimation, I generated simulated spike trains using the LNP model with known ground-truth receptive fields.
Since the true receptive field is already known, applying Spike-Triggered Average should recover it accurately. As shown here, the recovered filters closely match the ground truth, confirming that the implementation behaves as expected.

:::


## Controllable cortical cultures as a biological surrogate


::: {.columns}

::: {.column .fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="1" width="50%"}
#### Dissociated cortical cultures from mice
![](images/025x_3C_10x_objective_center_yfp.jpg){width="100%"}
:::
::: {.column .fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="2" width="50%"}
#### Optogenetics
<div class="r-stack">
![](images/optogeentics_1.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%"}

![](images/optogeentics_2.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="3" width="100%"}

</div>
:::
:::

<div class="" style="position:absolute; bottom:0px; right:20px; font-size:0.6em; color:gray;">
Deisseroth et al. (2012)
</div>

::: notes
The second requirement was to establish a controllable biological model.
For this, I used dissociated cortical neurons isolated from the cerebral hemispheres of postnatal mice. These neurons were cultured on high-density multielectrode arrays, where they self-organize into functional two-dimensional neuronal networks.
The multielectrode array allows simultaneous recording of extracellular electrical activity from many locations across the culture. The fluorescence image shown here illustrates one such mature neuronal network.

The next question is how to stimulate these neurons in a precise and reproducible manner.
Although electrical stimulation is widely used, it lacks cellular specificity and often introduces stimulation artifacts into the recordings.
Instead, I use optogenetics, a non-invasive technique that enables precise optical control of genetically targeted neurons with excellent spatial and temporal resolution.
In this approach, neurons are transduced with a viral vector expressing light-sensitive ion channels, known as opsins. When illuminated with light of the appropriate wavelength, these channels open and depolarize the neuron, generating action potentials.
In this work, I use the green-light-sensitive excitatory channelrhodopsin called ChReef, which provides reliable optical activation of the cultured neurons.


:::

::: notes
As I mentioned earlier, several experimental platforms already exist for combining optogenetic stimulation with electrophysiological recordings. This figure shows one such long-term stimulation setup.
Using this system, it is possible to estimate receptive fields. However, the recovered STAs primarily localize the positions of active neurons and do not resolve fine cellular or subcellular features. In other words, the spatial resolution of the stimulation becomes the limiting factor.
To probe receptive fields at much finer scales, a new experimental platform was required.
:::

This led to four major design requirements:
First, optical stimulation with cellular to subcellular spatial resolution.

::: notes
The result is the HD-MANTIS platform—High-Density Microelectrode Array-based Neuronal Targeting via Illuminated Stimuli—which integrates high-resolution optical stimulation with large-scale electrophysiological recording. 
The system consists of three main components.
The first, and most important, is the optical stimulation module. It is based on a microscope-like optical path, where the illumination source is a high-definition monochrome green OLED display. The display contains approximately two million pixels, each about 6 micrometres in size, enabling highly precise spatial patterning of light.
The second component is the control system, built around a Raspberry Pi. It generates the stimulation patterns through its HDMI interface while its programmable GPIO pins provide hardware triggering and synchronization with the recording system.
Finally, neuronal activity is recorded using the Maxwell high-density microelectrode array platform, which provides approximately one thousand simultaneous recording channels with an electrode pitch of 17.5 micrometres.

Having introduced the overall architecture of the HD-MANTIS system, I will now demonstrate how the key engineering requirements defined earlier were achieved and experimentally validated.

:::

::: {.columns}

#### Response verification {.fragment .fade.in data-fragment-index="1"}

![](images/stim_irr_verf.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%"}

![](images/stim_irr_verf_rec.png){.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="3" width="100%"}

#### Different Lenses {.fragment .fade.in data-fragment-index="4"}
::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="5"}
<canvas class="lens-chart" width="900" height="800"></canvas>

:::

:::

:::

:::

<div style="margin-top:-30px;">
::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="3"}
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{LPD} = 0.013~\mathrm{mW}/\mathrm{mm}^2
}
$$
:::
</div>

::: notes
Every opsin requires a minimum light intensity to evoke neuronal activity. However, the activation threshold of the ChReef variant used in this work has not been well characterized.
To determine this threshold, I transduced cortical cultures with ChReef and illuminated them using full-field flashes with a controlled duty cycle while recording the electrophysiological response.
Here, the electrode trace shows robust action potentials that are tightly time-locked to the optical stimulus, confirming that the delivered light intensity is sufficient to activate the opsin.
Having established the required optical power, I then characterized different objective lenses. The measured light intensity follows the expected inverse-square dependence on the lens f-number. Based on these measurements, I selected a 16 mm triplet lens, which provides the required optical power while meeting the system's design constraints.

:::


## Optical system charecterisation

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}

#### Different Lenses 

<canvas class="lens-chart" width="900" height="800"></canvas>



::: {.fragment #show-points }
:::

::: {.fragment #show-fit }
:::

::: {.fragment #highlight-point}
:::


<div class="stack-eq" style="margin-top:55px;">
::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="1"}
$$
\boxed{
\text{Theoretical Limit}~:~1.9 \mu\mathrm{m}
}
$$
:::
</div>
:::


::: {.column width="60%"}

#### On-axis Point Spread Function
<div class="r-stack">

![](images/psf_on_axis.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%"}

![](images/psf_on_axis_fits.png){.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="3" width="100%"}

</div>

<div class="stack-eq" style="margin-top:-30px;">
::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="4"}
$$
\boxed{
\text{On-axis FWHM}~:~10.8 \mu\mathrm{m}
}
$$
:::
</div>
:::

:::


::: notes
Every opsin requires a minimum light intensity to evoke neuronal activity. However, the activation threshold of the ChReef variant used in this work has not been well characterized.
To determine this threshold, I transduced cortical cultures with ChReef and illuminated them using full-field flashes with a controlled duty cycle while recording the electrophysiological response.
Here, the electrode trace shows robust action potentials that are tightly time-locked to the optical stimulus, confirming that the delivered light intensity is sufficient to activate the opsin.
Having established the required optical power, I then characterized different objective lenses. The measured light intensity follows the expected inverse-square dependence on the lens f-number. Based on these measurements, I selected a 16 mm triplet lens, which provides the required optical power while meeting the system's design constraints.

Delivering sufficient optical power alone is not enough. To stimulate individual neurons, the system must also provide adequate spatial resolution.
Although the optical design predicts that each OLED pixel can be projected to approximately 1.9 micrometres, this assumes an ideal lens system.
In practice, optical aberrations broaden the projected spot. To quantify this effect, I measured the point spread function across the field of view.
By fitting Gaussian profiles to each measured spot, I estimated the full width at half maximum, which represents the practical optical resolution of the system.
The measurements show a practical resolution of approximately 11 micrometres. They also reveal increasing aberrations toward the edges of the field, whereas the on-axis spot remains nearly symmetric.
:::

::: notes
Since receptive field estimation using Spike-Triggered Average assumes uncorrelated inputs, the primary stimulus used in this work is the Poisson–Bernoulli stimulus.

Each frame consists of a binary pattern defined by two parameters: the stimulus block size, which determines the spatial resolution, and the activation probability, PonP_{\mathrm{on}}Pon​, which controls the fraction of illuminated blocks in each frame.

As shown here, decreasing the block size increases the spatial resolution, while changing PonP_{\mathrm{on}}Pon​ controls the sparsity of the stimulus.

Choosing these parameters involves a trade-off. The stimulus should be sparse enough to isolate individual neurons, yet sufficiently dense to provide enough variability for reliable receptive field estimation. This is kept in mind while doing experiments.
:::

::: notes
The third stimulus mode is an oriented grating generator, which is designed to probe the orientation stimulus selectivity of neurons.
These stimuli are generated directly on the GPU using programmable shaders. Rather than storing each frame explicitly, the shader computes the intensity of every pixel from a mathematical function describing a sinusoidal grating.
By varying the orientation, spatial wavelength, and spatial frequency of the grating, a wide range of visual stimuli can be generated efficiently in real time.
Here, I show examples of gratings with different orientations and spatial wavelengths that can be presented during experiments.
Together with the poisson bernoulli stimulus the software stack is capable of performing key experiments.

## Frame times as a sync signal
Frame times are logged directly from the GPU

::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Setup
![](images/sync/sync_setup.png){.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="1" width="100%" fig-align="center"}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Oscilloscope traces
<div class="r-stack">

![](images/sync/sync1.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%" fig-align="center"}

![](images/sync/sync2.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="3" width="100%" fig-align="center"}
</div>
:::


::: notes
The next engineering requirement is precise synchronization between the stimulation and recording systems.
Since the optical display and the electrophysiology hardware operate on independent clocks, they do not naturally share a common time base. For receptive field estimation, where spike timing is compared to the presented stimulus with millisecond precision, accurate synchronization is essential.
To achieve this, a digital synchronization pulse is generated every time a stimulus frame is presented and transmitted directly to the Maxwell recording system.
I first validated this approach using periodic flashing stimuli. A photodiode measured the actual light output of the display, while an oscilloscope simultaneously recorded the synchronization pulses. As shown here, the synchronization events closely match the timing of the optical stimulus.
For more realistic stimuli, such as the Poisson–Bernoulli sequences, the frame intervals are no longer perfectly periodic because of small computational fluctuations during frame generation. These fluctuations are approximately 1 millisecond, as shown by the distribution of synchronization intervals.

:::


## Synchronisation quality

::: {.column width="50%"}
- For aligment a linear transformation between stimulus events and recorded events was performed

$$
t_{\mathrm{rec}} = \mathrm{a}~ t_{\mathrm{stim}} + \mathrm{b}
$$


- Residuals were measured as

$$
\mathrm{residual} = t_{\mathrm{mea}} - {t_{\mathrm{rec}}}
$$

and grouped as 
<span style="color:#5470C6;">< $1~\mathrm{ms}$ </span>,
<span style="color:#91CC75;">< $2~\mathrm{ms}$ </span> and
<span style="color:#EE6666;">< $5~\mathrm{ms}$ </span> 

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

<div id="barplot" style="width:900px;height:600px;"></div>

::: {.fragment #bar-reveal-1}
:::
::: {.fragment #bar-reveal-2}
:::
::: {.fragment #bar-reveal-3}
:::
:::

::: notes
The important question, however, is how accurately these events are captured by the recording system.
To quantify this, I aligned the stimulus timestamps with the recorded synchronization events and calculated the residual timing error.
Across multiple recordings, more than 98% of synchronization events were recorded with an error below 1 millisecond, demonstrating that the system provides reliable temporal alignment for receptive field mapping experiments.

:::

## Results - Recording fidelity of the Maxwell System
::: {.column width="60%"}
#### Spontaneous activity DIV 20
![](images/results/spontaneous_activity_P004474_DIV20_100s.png){.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="1" width="100%" fig-align="left"}
:::

::: {.column .fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="2" width="40%"}
#### Analysis
- Only units with > 1000 spikes are selected for analysis
- All STAs are z-scored as
$$
\hat{k}(\mathbf{x}, \tau_k) = \frac{k(\mathbf{x}, \tau_k) - \mu_k}{\sigma_k}
$$
:::

::: notes
Before discussing receptive fields, I would first like to demonstrate the recording quality of the platform.
This recording was obtained from a 20-day-old cortical culture. Each colour represents activity recorded from a different electrode, illustrating the large-scale parallel recordings that are possible with the Maxwell system.
For the remainder of this presentation, I will focus on recording units that produced at least 1000 spikes, since reliable STA estimation requires sufficient spike counts.

The activation probability, Pon was chosen to provide a balance between stimulus sparsity and information content. It is low enough to selectively stimulate small regions, yet high enough to maintain sufficient stimulus variability for reliable receptive field estimation.

Finally, all receptive fields are displayed as z-score normalized STAs to improve visualization of the underlying structure.

:::

## Increasing stimulus resolution increase STA features
::: {.column width="55%"}
<div class="r-stack">
![](images/results/res_control/master_res_control.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.column width="45%"}
- Experiment duration : 15 min
- Approx spikes collected  : ~ 2000
- $p_{\mathrm{on}}$ = 0.1
- STA noise decreases by ~ $1/\sqrt{N_s}$
:::

::: notes
My first experiment investigates how stimulus resolution affects receptive field estimation.
Here, the stimulus block size is progressively decreased while keeping the activation probability fixed at 0.1.
As the stimulus resolution increases, progressively finer receptive field structures become visible.
However, another important factor is the number of recorded spikes. Since the variance of the STA decreases proportionally to 1/N1/\sqrt{N}1/N​, longer recordings substantially improve the quality of the recovered receptive fields.


This motivated the long-duration experiments that I will show next.

:::

::: notes
Long-duration recordings reveal highly complex spatiotemporal receptive fields.  Here I show four representative examples.

Unlike conventional receptive fields that primarily localize neuronal position, these measurements reveal extended spatial structures.
Long-duration recordings reveal highly structured spatiotemporal receptive fields.

Some of the fine, localized features may reflect the morphology of the recorded neuron. Since the optogenetic actuator is expressed throughout the neuronal membrane, including dendritic processes, optical stimulation may capture responses originating from different parts of the same cell.

However, larger-scale structures extending well beyond the dimensions of a single neuron are unlikely to represent morphology alone and more likely reflect network-mediated interactions or indirect activation through neighbouring neurons.

:::

<div class="r-stack">

![](images/results/Inh_subfields/master_inh_str_1.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1" width="100%" fig-align="center"}

![](images/results/Inh_subfields/master_inh_str_2.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%" fig-align="center"}

![](images/results/Inh_subfields/master_inh_str_4.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="4" width="100%" fig-align="center"}

</div>
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
<div class="r-stack">
![](images/results/Inh_subfields/zoomed_inh_1.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1" width="100%" fig-align="center"}

![](images/results/Inh_subfields/zoomed_inh_2.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2" width="100%" fig-align="center"}

![](images/results/Inh_subfields/zoomed_inh_3.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="3" width="100%" fig-align="center"}

</div>


:::

::: notes
Another interesting observation is the presence of inhibitory substructures.
These appear as negative regions within the STA, indicating that stimulation of nearby locations suppresses the probability of firing.
A plausible explanation is that optogenetic stimulation activates inhibitory interneurons, which subsequently suppress the recorded unit through the surrounding network.
The diffuse appearance of these structures, even for recordings with very high spike counts, suggests that these responses are dominated by network interactions rather than direct optical activation.

:::

## Electrical structure reveals correlations to the STA

::: {.column width="50%"}

#### Localization of STA 

<div class="r-stack">

<div class="fragment fade-out stack-frame" data-fragment-index="2">
![](images/results/electrical_foot/sta_ef_1.png){width="100%"}
</div>

![](images/results/electrical_foot/sta_ef_2.png){width="80%"}
</div>

</div>
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

#### Electrical footprint

<div class="r-stack">



<div class="fragment fade-in-then-out stack-frame " data-fragment-index="4">
![](images/results/electrical_foot/ef_ef_1.png){width="80%"}
<div class="stack-eq">
$$
\bbox[0px,border:0px solid white]{\color{red}{\bar{v}_i(\alpha)}}=
\frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{s=1}^{N_s}v_i(t_s+\alpha) \quad \alpha \in [-2,2]~\textrm{ms}
$$
</div>
</div>

<div class="fragment fade-in stack-frame" data-fragment-index="5">
![](images/results/electrical_foot/ef_ef_2.png){width="80%"}
</div>

</div>

:::

::: notes
The extended receptive fields naturally raise the question of whether they correspond to the physical morphology of the recorded neuron. 
To investigate this, I first localized the receptive field using its peak response.
I then computed the spike-triggered electrical footprint by averaging extracellular action potentials recorded across neighbouring electrodes.
The peak-to-peak amplitudes produce an electrical image that approximates the morphology of the recorded unit.
Comparing these electrical images with the optical receptive fields reveals several structural similarities, suggesting that the recovered receptive fields may indeed capture aspects of neuronal morphology.

:::

## Preliminary results for orientation selectivity

<div class="unit-grid">

<div class="chart-panel">
<canvas id="unit870"></canvas>
</div>

<div class="chart-panel">
<canvas id="unit787"></canvas>
</div>

<div class="chart-panel">
<canvas id="unit970"></canvas>
</div>

<div class="chart-panel">
<canvas id="unit890"></canvas>
</div>

</div>

::: {.fragment #show-scatter}
:::

::: {.fragment #show-mean}
:::

::: notes
Finally, I'd like to show a preliminary result demonstrating the flexibility of the platform.

Here, instead of random stimuli, I presented drifting sinusoidal gratings at different orientations and measured the firing rate of individual recording units.

In this example, the cell responds much more strongly to gratings oriented at 45° and 225° than to other orientations. This preference is consistent across repeated trials, as shown by the trial-by-trial responses and the average tuning curve.

This is a surprising observation. In a dissociated cortical culture, there is no organized visual map or predefined orientation architecture as found in the visual cortex. Nevertheless, some neurons exhibit clear orientation preferences.

One possible explanation is spontaneous symmetry breaking within the cultured network. This asymmetry could arise from the neuron's own morphology—for example, an asymmetric dendritic arbor—or from an asymmetric arrangement of its presynaptic inputs. At this stage, these remain hypotheses that require further investigation.
:::

## Conclusions
- Designed and validated a cellular-resolution optical stimulation system using reverse correlation.
- Integrated stimulation and high-density recording for medium-to-high throughput receptive field mapping.
- Revealed detailed receptive field structure, including correlations with neuronal electrical morphology.
- Preliminary evidence of orientation-selectivity.

::: notes
To conclude, this thesis has demonstrated the development of HD-MANTIS, a high-resolution optogenetic stimulation platform integrated with high-density electrophysiological recordings.
The platform was experimentally validated with respect to optical performance, software control, synchronization, and biological compatibility.
Using this system, I recovered spatiotemporal receptive fields at a spatial resolution that has not previously been explored in this experimental paradigm.
The recovered structures suggest that high-resolution optogenetic stimulation may reveal not only functional receptive fields but also aspects of neuronal morphology and network organization.
I believe this platform provides a flexible and cost-effective foundation for future studies investigating the relationship between neuronal structure and function.

:::

## Limitations and Future work

- Improve optical resolution through refinement of the stimulation optics and optical alignment.
- Implement hardware-based synchronization for robust timing between stimulation and recording.
- Calibrate stimulus localization to precisely align projected stimuli with the recording array.
- Adopt template-based spike sorting to improve single-cell isolation and increase the accuracy of receptive field and electrical structure analyses.

## Appendix - Resolution measurements

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

#### On-axis Point Spread Function
<div class="r-stack">

![](images/psf_on_axis.png){.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1" width="100%"}

![](images/psf_on_axis_fits.png){.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="2" width="100%"}

</div>

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

#### Spatial Inhomogeneity of the PSFs

![](images/psf_spatial_dist.png){.fragment width="100%" fig-align="center"}

:::

:::
::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="2"}
<div style="margin-top:-60px;">
$$
\boxed{
\text{On-axis FWHM}~:~10.8 \mu\mathrm{m}
}
$$
</div>
:::


::: notes
Delivering sufficient optical power alone is not enough. To stimulate individual neurons, the system must also provide adequate spatial resolution.
Although the optical design predicts that each OLED pixel can be projected to approximately 1.9 micrometres, this assumes an ideal lens system.
In practice, optical aberrations broaden the projected spot. To quantify this effect, I measured the point spread function across the field of view.
By fitting Gaussian profiles to each measured spot, I estimated the full width at half maximum, which represents the practical optical resolution of the system.
The measurements show a practical resolution of approximately 11 micrometres. They also reveal increasing aberrations toward the edges of the field, whereas the on-axis spot remains nearly symmetric.
:::

::: notes
 the next requirement was a flexible software system capable of generating precisely controlled optical stimuli.
To achieve this, I developed a modular software backend. The user specifies an experiment through a simple Python interface, where all stimulus parameters are defined. These parameters are then passed to a C-based rendering engine that interfaces directly with the graphics hardware to generate the stimulus frames in real time.
The generated frames are displayed on the OLED, while their presentation times are simultaneously transmitted as digital synchronization events to the Maxwell recording system. This ensures that every presented frame can be accurately aligned with the recorded neuronal activity during offline analysis.

:::
